name: Ancient ox-gall hair dye (Assyrian)

lead: Assyrian clay tablets from the 7th century BCE describe a preparation to turn gray hair black. According to Wikipedia's hair coloring article, the ingredients were the gall of a black ox, cypress oil, licorice and honey [1].
It is one of the earliest documented gray-hair remedies, alongside Egyptian recipes in the Ebers Papyrus from around 1550 BCE [1]. It interests people studying the long history of covering gray hair.

paras: Only the ingredient list is described in the cited source; no modern practice or method is documented. Dyes in antiquity were often plant-based, such as henna, indigo and black walnut hulls [1].
No modern safety or effectiveness data exist for this recipe, and it is not a current product.

angle.text: The tablets present it as a way to turn gray hair black. It is a historical record rather than an available product.

lead: Wikipedia records that Assyrian clay tablets of the 7th century BCE mention using the gall of a black ox, cypress oil, licorice and honey to turn gray hair black [1]. The goal was cosmetic: darkening gray hair to a youthful color.

The source places it among very old cosmetic records: Assyrian herbals from around 2177 BCE are cited as holding some of the oldest known cosmetic recipes including hair dye, and the Ebers Papyrus of about 1550 BCE has Egyptian recipes for dyeing gray hair and eyebrows [1].
No modern study has tested this particular recipe.

paras: Ancient hair coloring used mostly plant materials including henna, indigo, cassia, senna, turmeric, amla and black walnut hulls, as well as red ochre [1]. Greek historian Diodorus Siculus described Celts bleaching their hair with lime [1].
